newsitem.title: NIGERIA: Nigeria softens Commonwealth by freeing three men.
newsitem.headline: Nigeria softens Commonwealth by freeing three men.

text.p: Nigeria military authorities, who are facing pressure to restore democracy and to respect human rights, have freed three human rights lawyers as a Commonwealth mission met Nigerian officials in the capital Abuja.

Opposition activists hailed the release of activists Gani Fawehinmi, Femi Falana and Femi Aborishade on Tuesday after nearly a year in jail without trial but said it was timed to stave off any new Commonwealth action against Nigeria.
"The same thing happened in May, this piece-meal release of political detainees," said one.
When Nigerian officials met the Commonwealth Ministerial Action Group (CMAG) in London in May half a dozen long-term political detainees were freed back home.

CMAG, set up to nudge Nigeria towards observing the Commonwealth's Harare declaration of good governance, then decided to suspend the imposition of agreed sanctions on Nigeria to allow for more talks with the Abuja government.
CMAG was set up at the last Commonwealth summit in Auckland, New Zealand, where Nigeria was suspended for hanging nine minority rights activists including writer Ken Saro-Wiwa.

CMAG ministers, led by their chairman Zimbabwean Foreign Minister Stan Mudenge met behind closed doors with a 20-member Nigerian delegation led by Foreign Minister Tom Ikimi, who pulled no punches in his opening remarks.
"Nigeria considers the immediate lifting of her suspension from the Commonwealth as the only means for restoring confidence and mutual understanding between us and the Commonwealth," Ikimi said.
CMAG is made up of foreign ministers of Britain, Canada, New Zealand, South Africa, Zimbabwe, Ghana, Jamaica and Malaysia and its report will be submitted to the Commonwealth secretariat in London.
"Both sides are prepared and willing to advance the dialogue and to ensure that Nigeria is re-instated in the Commonwealth," Ghana deputy foreign minister Mohammed Chambas told reporters.
The CMAG ministers met Nigerian ruler General Sani Abacha late on Tuesday.
Their meetings on Wednesday, the second and last day of their talks in Nigeria, will include the electoral commission and the civil rights commission.
Nigeria, Africa's most populous nation with 100 million people, has been in turmoil since June 1993 when the army annulled a presidential election in spite of pledges to restore democracy.
Among many people still in detention are Moshood Abiola, the wealthy businessman presumed to have won the annulled poll.

Worldwide appeals for Abiola to be freed have been rebuffed and the authorities insist he will face trial for treason for proclaiming himself president in 1994 in defiance of Abacha, who seized power in the chaos that followed the annulment.
Abacha has promised to hand over to a democratically-elected president in 1998 but the Commonwealth wants a handover before next year's summit of the group in Edinburgh, Scotland.
Nigeria, which says its own transition programme is on course, is unlikely to accept any change to it.
